name: CAD/CAM spinal brace

card.summary: A custom spinal brace designed from a 3D body scan and milled or printed by computer, used to hold an adolescent's curved spine from progressing so the back and torso stay more symmetrical as they grow.
card.aka: Custom spinal brace; computer-designed scoliosis brace
card.note: A medical device prescribed and fitted by an orthotist for scoliosis in growing adolescents; it is worn for many hours a day until growth ends.

quick.overview:
A CAD/CAM spinal brace is a rigid torso brace for scoliosis (a sideways curve of the spine) that is designed on a computer from a scan or measurements of the body, instead of from a plaster cast. It is made by carving a foam model or by 3D printing. The appearance payoff is that bracing during growth aims to stop a curve from getting larger, which keeps the shoulders, ribcage and waist more even.

The computer design lets orthotists adjust pressure pads and relief areas virtually and repeat a design precisely. Studies of these braces report in-brace curve correction, lighter and thinner shells that cover less of the trunk, and patient preference data; a randomized trial followed 120 adolescents for two years.
quick.how: An orthotist measures or scans the torso, a clinician or technician edits the 3D shape on screen, and the brace is produced by milling a foam mould over which plastic is formed, or by printing it. It is then fitted, checked on X-ray and adjusted. Conventional thoracolumbosacral braces are typically recommended for around 22 to 23 hours a day until growth ends, and teams follow up with periodic X-rays.
quick.risks: Braces can cause skin irritation, discomfort and self-consciousness, and wearing them for many hours a day is demanding. Effectiveness depends on fit, design and how consistently the brace is worn. Bracing is a medical treatment decided with a spine specialist, usually for curves in a defined range in patients who are still growing.

lead: A CAD/CAM spinal brace is a custom-made orthosis for spinal curvature, most often adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, whose shape is designed with computer-aided design (CAD) and produced by computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) such as carving or 3D printing, rather than being moulded over a plaster cast [3][4]. It belongs to the family of thoracolumbosacral orthoses (TLSOs), the rigid torso braces that include the Boston and Milwaukee designs [9][10].

The appearance-related goal is indirect but concrete. Bracing in a growing adolescent is intended to hold a curve from progressing, which keeps the spine, shoulder line, ribcage and waist closer to symmetrical in adulthood [9]. Researchers have also described CAD/CAM designs as lighter, thinner and covering less of the trunk than traditional shells, which people may find easier to wear and to hide under clothing [1].

Published work includes a single-centre randomized controlled trial of 120 adolescents comparing CAD/CAM braces with and without finite element modelling [1], a ten-patient comparison with plaster-moulded braces [2], early reports of a CAD/CAM design [5], and a 2026 study of pattern-specific CAD-CAM braces across curve types [6].

angle.text: The brace is worn during growth to limit curve progression, which preserves the symmetry of the back and torso. Computer design allows thinner, lighter shells that are easier to wear under clothes.

paras: Traditional scoliosis braces are made by wrapping the torso in plaster or similar material to take a cast, then shaping a positive mould and forming plastic over it. Authors of the CAD/CAM literature note that computer systems were introduced partly to reduce physical contact and the variability of an individual orthotist's skills [5]. In CAD/CAM production the body shape is captured digitally, the orthotist edits it virtually, and the brace is usually made by carving a polyurethane foam model over which polyethylene or polypropylene is vacuum-formed. A 2017 workflow paper describes this process and outlines how 3D printing could replace the carving step [3].
Some designs add finite element modelling, a simulation of how forces from the brace act on the spine and trunk, to refine pad placement before the brace is made [1].

Scoliosis changes the outline of the torso, and adolescents often consider asymmetry of shoulders, ribs or waist the most visible feature. The goal of bracing in a growing patient is to prevent the curve from getting worse, and a review of the condition notes that evidence supports this effect, while whether bracing improves appearance is unclear [9]. The same review lists curve size and skeletal maturity among the factors used to decide who is braced [9].

The authors of the randomized trial describe earlier work in which CAD/CAM and finite element designs produced promising in-brace corrections and were lighter, thinner and covered less trunk surface [1].

A single-centre randomized controlled trial assigned 120 adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis who met Scoliosis Research Society brace criteria to braces designed with CAD/CAM (61 patients) or with CAD/CAM plus finite element modelling (59 patients), and assessed clinical outcomes, 3D correction, compliance and quality of life at two years [1][7].

A ten-patient study with an average starting Cobb angle of 30.8 degrees gave each patient both a plaster-moulded and a CAD/CAM TLSO, measured in-brace correction after three weeks of 23-hour daily wear, and asked patients which brace they preferred after three months [2]. A preliminary report examined a CAD/CAM design called the Los Angeles brace [5]. A 2026 study looked at treatment outcomes of a pattern-specific CAD-CAM brace across different curve patterns and severities [6]. A systematic review has examined the Chêneau brace, a pattern-specific design, for curve progression and control [8].

Orthosis articles describe discomfort, skin irritation and low self-esteem as long-standing problems with rigid braces [9]. Results depend on brace design, the orthotist's skill and how consistently the brace is worn [9]. A night-only brace is another option whose comparative effectiveness is being studied [9].

timeline.event: Early reports compare CAD/CAM and plaster-moulded TLSOs and describe the Los Angeles CAD/CAM brace [2][5].
A workflow paper describes CAD/CAM brace adjustment and the prospects for 3D printing [3].
A randomized trial reports two-year results for CAD/CAM braces with and without finite element modelling [1].
A study reports outcomes of a pattern-specific CAD-CAM brace across curve types [6].
